subject: Density estimation in R with multiple covariates

messages.author: b4e5d185d14e5d19
messages.subject: Density estimation in R with multiple covariates
parts:
Hi,

I want to get density estimates for individual species from a multi-year bird survey (line transects), using year, observer, and cluster size as covariates as I have reason to believe that each might affect a species' detectability.  Ultimately, I would like to run the model: ds(data, ... , cutpoints = c(0,15,35,55,75,105,145), ... , formula = ~ as.factor(year) + as.factor(observer) + size).

Year
I think that year is affecting species' detectability because when I plotted detection function for each species with year as a covariate to see whether detection functions were different in each year and found that for many species the shape of the detection function was markedly different. However, this could be an artefact of having different observers in each year. I chose to use year as a covariate rather than doing full stratification by year (i.e. getting a separate detection function for each year) because the latter approach greatly limited the number of species with sufficient number observations (60 observations per stratum). 

Observer
I have five years of data, and in each year two to three different teams conducted surveys, with essentially no overlap between teams in different years, giving 12 unique observer team IDs. Differences is observer effort and skill level can obviously lead to different biases in how species are detected, so I'd like to account for that.

Cluster size
I used cluster size as a covariate because I want to account for cluster-size bias (larger flock sizes are more likely to be detected at further distances).

Problems:

1.) I am able to run ds models when my flatfile contains year as the only covariate (with columns 'Region.Label', 'Area', 'Sample.Label', 'Effort', 'distance', 'size', 'year', and 'species'). When I add an 'observer' column to my flatfile (with columns 'Region.Label', 'Area', 'Sample.Label', 'Effort', 'observer', 'distance', 'size', 'year', and 'species') and run the same model (with year as the only covariate), I get errors saying all models failed to fit/no models could be fitted. This tells me that adding an 'observer' column somehow messes up the flatfile and I cannot figure why this might be. I'd appreciate any ideas!

2.) Also, how should I assess model fit? I am using manually defined cutpoints/bins (6 in total) because of heaping of 'exact' distance estimates, and when year is used as a covariate there are 5 levels (2012-2016) so there are no remaining degrees of freedom for a chi-square goodness of fit test. 

Thanks very much,
Michelle

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Density estimation in R with multiple covariates
parts:
Michelle

Sounds like a challenging dataset and you are trying to do a conscientious analysis.

First the easy question (1): "observer" is a reserved covariate name.  the ds() function sits on top of the machinery for doing mark-recapture distance sampling, where double observers are employed for the purposes of estimating g(0).  The simple solution is to rename that covariate "team" or some-such.

Harder question--measuring fit when the model being fitted has more parameters than points of support in the data.  No easy solution.  There is old literature on something called 'smearing' that essentially smooths through heaped detections (sect 7.4.3.4 of Buckland et al. (2001)).  However the methods for performing smearing are all ad-hoc, without a theoretical foundation.

Lastly, an unasked question: your description leads me to think that "team" and "year" are highly collinear (explaining similar sources of variation).  That will cause fitting problems and likely messy estimates of the parameters of the detection function.  First impressions are that using only "team" might be the way forward--assuming teams were spatial allocated so as not to mess spatial and team effects.

Hi Distance group,

Eric Rexstad recently helped me follow up on my original question regarding cluster size bias using observation team as a covariate (with a total of 10 different teams). I'd like to share this off-list exchange since posting my original question in case others have the same issue.

To summarise, he suggested that either adjustment terms or covariates should be used in a model, but not both, and he wrote code to test for cluster size bias in models with a multi-level factor covariate (attached). His code is written for a half normal key function but we also discuss what the code would look like for the hazard rate function. Other code available on this group addresses a similar issue but with two binary covariates.

Many thanks to Eric for taking the time to help!
Michelle

On Sat, Feb 18, 2017 at 12:37 AM, Eric Rexstad <er...@st-andrews.ac.uk> wrote:

Michelle

1--you need to get you head around the idea of dummy variables.  Simplest case, I want to record whether an observation is from a male or female.  I have 2 classes (male/female), yet I can record that in my data by simply indicating 0 for male and 1 for female (using only a single column in my data file).

Suppose I had 3 age classes (young, immature, mature); how do I need to record that; I can use the system 01-for young, 10-for immature, and 00-mature.  Three categories differentiated with 2 columns of binary variables.  

In each case, there is one level of my variable that is recorded with the absence of values (0-male and 00-mature).

In all applications of dummy variables there will be one level that is represented by all 0.  That is the team I designated as 'ZZZ' in the example I built for you.  But to interpret the coefficients estimated by ds(), you recognise this level ZZZ is associated with the "intercept-only" term in your model, because all other coefficients are associated with 0s.

Have a look at Wikipedia, in the section on ANOVA model with one qualitative variable.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dummy_variable_(statistics)

2--correct, that is the proper form for the hazard rate model

3--good job of working out how to access the estimated coefficients of the model.

On Fri, Feb 10, 2017 at 1:21 AM, Eric Rexstad <er...@st-andrews.ac.uk> wrote:

Michelle

I commend you on the thorough job of analysis.  There are a couple of ways you could go here; none are necessarily better than others.

I'll go backward and answer a question you didn't ask.  Looking at the coefficients (and SEs) of your team covariate, there are lots of teams (hence lots of parameters).  It is plausible for you to collapse some teams together based upon the story in the coefficient SEs.  For example, there are "fat" SEs for teams, JJM, KMR, MCE and NCR.  The interpretation of those coefficients with their SEs are that those teams have detection functions "equivalent" to the detection function for the "base" team (the first one in the dataset).  Problem is, that team pattern might differ among species.

If you have infinite time, you could consider combining those 4 teams along with the base team into a "metateam".  You would be asking ds() to fit a detection function with 4 fewer parameters.  Some of that imprecision in coefficient estimation is undoubtedly associated with some teams having few detections.

Second question you didn't ask.  I see you are using adjustment terms as well as covariates.  That is sometimes asking for trouble.  Adjustment terms are added to the key functions to fit occasional "wobbles" in the data.  Covariates do much the same job, except a more mechanistic approach is used--detectability varies by team, rather than detectability "wobbles" for unknown reasons, so add a polynomial kink to the function.  I have colleagues who are happy with both covariates and adjustment terms, but I argue for parsimonious models and would rather use covariates and omit adjustment terms.

Now for the question you *did* ask.  You did find a piece of code I wrote three years ago to perform the log(size) vs g(y) regression for a particular covariate model.  I could (or you could) modify the code to account for your multi-level team covariate.  I would probably pull back from the adjustment factor there as well.  What would be the consequence of this analysis?  I guess for species for which the slope coefficient of the regression is significant, you'd want to put size back into your detection function as a covariate.

Lots of work, but I guess that defines a PhD project.  Let me know if you want me to have a bash at the R script that performs the size vs g(y) regression.
